pos: n. (Josue de la Place, 1596–1665, professor at Saumur, who denied the immediate imputation of Adam's sin)
etymology: Hebrew Yehoshua, the LORD is salvation, through French Josue; de la Place, of the square.
biblical_def: Josue de la Place, latinised Placaeus, was pastor at Nantes and from 1633 professor of theology at the Protestant academy of Saumur, where he taught beside Moise Amyraut and Louis Cappel. In 1640 he published a thesis on original sin denying the immediate imputation of Adam's first sin to his posterity: men are born corrupt, he granted, and that corruption is from Adam and is itself culpable, but Adam's act is not reckoned to them antecedently to their own inherent depravity. The French national synod of Charenton in 1645 condemned the doctrine that denies imputation, and Placaeus protested that he had not been condemned, since he denied only the immediate imputation and held the mediate. The distinction was pressed by Jonathan Edwards the elder's opponents a century later and is still argued. The Reformed objection is that Paul's parallel requires the first: as Adam's one offence is reckoned, so Christ's one righteousness is reckoned. “For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous” (Rom 5:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines imputation as the attribution of anything to a person, and original sin as the depravity of nature derived from Adam.
webster_full: IMPUTA'TION, n. The act of imputing or charging; attribution, usually of evil.
ORIG'INAL, a. First in order; preceding all others; original sin, the depravity of our nature.
DEPRAV'ITY, n. Corruption; a vitiated state of moral character.
scriptures: Rom 5:19
For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.
Rom 5:12
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
Rom 5:18
Therefore as by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life.
For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.
corruption_summary: Saumur's professor, condemned at Charenton for denying immediate imputation.
corruption_paragraphs: The mediate-imputation scheme is attractive because it seems to answer the common objection that it is unjust to charge a man with another's act. It is also unstable, as its history shows: once the forensic link between Adam's act and our guilt is loosened, the same reasoning is applied to the second Adam, and imputed righteousness goes the way of imputed sin. That is not a slander on Placaeus, who held justification by faith; it is what happened to his successors.

The principle to recover is the symmetry Paul insists on, which is the whole argument of Romans 5: “as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous” (Rom 5:19). And “as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive” (1Co 15:22) — one representative act on each side, reckoned to those he stood for.
roots_summary: Greek logizomai (G3049), to reckon, impute; parakoe (G3876), disobedience; hupakoe (G5218), obedience.
roots_lines: Greek parakoe (G3876) — disobedience, failure to hear; Romans 5:19.
Greek kathistemi (G2525) — to constitute, make, appoint; Romans 5:19.
Greek dierchomai (G1330) — to pass through, pass upon; Romans 5:12.

“as by one man sin entered into the world” (Rom 5:12) — Placaeus granted the corruption.
“as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive” (1Co 15:22) — why the symmetry matters.

pos: n. (the Academy of Saumur, 1599–1685, the French Protestant academy on the Loire)
etymology: Greek Akademeia, Plato's grove at Athens; Saumur, the town on the Loire.
biblical_def: The Academy of Saumur was founded in 1599 by Philippe du Plessis-Mornay, Henri IV's Huguenot counsellor, and became the most brilliant and the most suspected of the French Protestant academies. Its first great name was the Scot John Cameron, and under his successors it produced a distinctive school: Moise Amyraut's hypothetical universalism, Josue de la Place's mediate imputation, and Louis Cappel's demonstration that the Hebrew vowel points are a late addition and not part of the inspired text. Each of the three was attacked from Geneva, Sedan and the Netherlands as a softening of orthodoxy, and the Helvetic Consensus Formula of 1675 was drawn up specifically to shut all three out of the Swiss churches. Saumur was not a liberal institution by any later measure — it held the Confession of La Rochelle and trained pastors for a persecuted church — but it was the place where the Reformed consensus was first probed from within, and the probing was serious. The academy was suppressed in 1685 with the revocation of the Edict of Nantes. “in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an academy as a school or seminary of learning, and orthodoxy as soundness of faith.
webster_full: ACAD'EMY, n. A school, or seminary of learning, holding a middle rank between a university and a common school.
OR'THODOXY, n. Soundness of faith; a belief in the genuine doctrines taught in the Scriptures.
FAC'ULTY, n. The members of a profession; the body of professors in a university.
scriptures: Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Jude 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: The French academy on the Loire that produced Amyraut, Placaeus and Cappel.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Saumur is a useful test case for how a confessional tradition should handle able men who press at its edges. Geneva's answer was the Helvetic Consensus, a new subscription barring the three positions; and there is something to be said for it, since each of the three did open a door later walked through. There is also something to be said against it, since Cappel was simply right about the vowel points.

The principle to recover is that the two duties stand together: a church must “earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jude 1:3), and its teachers must be workmen “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) — which sometimes means correcting what the church had assumed. Counsel in the plural is the safeguard (Pro 11:14), not a single academy or a single synod.
roots_summary: Hebrew yaats (H3289), to counsel; Greek orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight; epagonizomai (G1864), to contend earnestly.
roots_lines: Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, divide rightly; 2 Timothy 2:15.
usage: “in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14) — and Saumur was one counsellor.
“rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15) — Cappel on the vowel points.
“earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered” (Jude 1:3) — the Helvetic Consensus, 1675.

pos: n. (Cesar Malan, 1787–1864, Genevan preacher and hymnwriter, a founder of the Reveil)
etymology: Latin Caesar, a Roman family name; Malan, a Waldensian surname, from the Piedmontese valleys.
biblical_def: Cesar Malan was a regent of the college at Geneva, of Waldensian descent, who in 1816 preached a sermon on justification by faith alone before the Venerable Company of Pastors and was dismissed from his post for it. Geneva's established church had by then settled into a polite Socinianism in which the deity of Christ was not denied so much as never mentioned, and Malan's preaching of the ruin of man and free grace in Christ was taken as fanaticism. He built a chapel in his own garden, the Chapelle du Temoignage, was suspended from the ministry of the national church in 1823, and spent forty years preaching there and travelling through France, Belgium, Scotland and England. With the Haldanes' influence and alongside Merle d'Aubigne and the Monod brothers he was a founder of the Reveil, the Francophone evangelical awakening. He wrote over a thousand hymns, many still sung in French Protestant churches, and among his converts was John Duncan of Edinburgh. “For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a revival as renewed attention to religion after decline, and a hymn as a song in honour of God.
webster_full: REVI'VAL, n. Renewed attention to religion, after indifference and decline.
HYMN, n. A song or ode in honor of God; a sacred lyric.
SUSPEND', v.t. To debar from any privilege, or from the execution of an office, for a time.
scriptures: Act 4:20
For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.
Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
Psa 40:3
And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God: many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD.
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
corruption_summary: The Genevan dismissed in 1816 for preaching justification by faith, and founder of the Reveil.
corruption_paragraphs: Malan's Geneva is the standing example of how a church loses the gospel without ever voting against it. No synod repudiated the deity of Christ or the atonement; the Company of Pastors simply agreed in 1817 that these subjects should not be treated in the pulpit, in the interest of peace. A generation of Genevans grew up hearing moral instruction in Calvin's own city.

The principle to recover is that silence on the central things is itself a denial, and that the apostolic answer to an order of silence is not negotiation: “For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20). The gospel is the power of God unto salvation (Rom 1:16), and a pulpit that will not name it has nothing else to offer.
roots_summary: Greek dunamai (G1410), to be able; dunamis (G1411), power; Hebrew chadash (H2319), new.
roots_lines: Greek dunamai (G1410) — to be able, to have power; Acts 4:20.
Hebrew tehillah (H8416) — praise, a song of praise; Psalm 40:3.
usage: “we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard” (Act 4:20) — Geneva, 1816.
“I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ” (Rom 1:16) — the sermon that cost him his post.
“he hath put a new song in my mouth” (Psa 40:3) — a thousand hymns.

pos: n. (Jean-Henri Merle d'Aubigne, 1794–1872, Genevan historian of the Reformation)
etymology: French merle, a blackbird; d'Aubigne, of Aubigne, a family name taken from his mother's line.
biblical_def: Jean-Henri Merle d'Aubigne was a Genevan of Huguenot descent, converted under Robert Haldane's Romans lectures in 1817, who studied at Berlin under Neander, served the French congregation at Hamburg and the Protestant church at Brussels, and in 1831 became professor of church history in the new evangelical theological school at Geneva founded by the men of the Reveil. His History of the Reformation of the Sixteenth Century, published from 1835, and the later History of the Reformation in Europe in the Time of Calvin, were among the most widely read books of the nineteenth century: translated into every European language, sold in hundreds of thousands in Britain and America, and responsible more than any other work for the Victorian English-speaking world's picture of Luther and Calvin. His method was archival and his tone frankly partisan; later scholarship has corrected much of his detail and nothing of his central judgment. He wrote to make a forgetful church remember. “This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines history as a narration of facts in the order in which they happened, and a chronicle as a historical account of facts in the order of time.
webster_full: HIS'TORY, n. An account of facts, particularly of facts respecting nations or states.
CHRON'ICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
NARRA'TIVE, n. The recital of a story; a relation of the particulars of an event.
scriptures: This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
Rom 15:4
For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.
One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.
corruption_summary: The Genevan whose History of the Reformation taught the nineteenth century its Luther.
corruption_paragraphs: Merle d'Aubigne is now cited chiefly as a warning about partisan history, and the criticism is fair as far as it goes: he wrote to edify as well as to record, he is credulous at points, and his Luther is a hero. What his critics less often grant is that the alternative then on offer was not neutrality but a rationalist history which treated the Reformation as a stage in the progress of free thought, and that was further from the sources than he was.

The principle to recover is that remembrance is a commanded use of the past: “whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope” (Rom 15:4) is said of Scripture, and the same logic drives the church's own annals. “One generation shall praise thy works to another” (Psa 145:4) requires somebody to write them down.
roots_summary: Hebrew kathab (H3789), to write; saphar (H5608), to recount; Greek didaskalia (G1319), teaching, learning.
usage: “This shall be written for the generation to come” (Psa 102:18) — the History, from 1835.
“written for our learning” (Rom 15:4) — his purpose in writing.
“One generation shall praise thy works to another” (Psa 145:4) — hundreds of thousands of copies.

pos: n. (Abraham Capadose, 1795–1874, Dutch physician of Portuguese Jewish descent, a leader of the Dutch Reveil)
etymology: Hebrew Abraham, father of a multitude; Capadose, a Sephardic family name of Portuguese origin.
biblical_def: Abraham Capadose was born in Amsterdam of a wealthy Portuguese Jewish family, took his medical degree at Leiden, and there with his cousin Isaac da Costa came under the teaching of the poet Willem Bilderdijk. Both were baptised in 1822, a conversion that cost them their place in the Jewish community and made them the most conspicuous figures of the Dutch Reveil, the awakening that revived orthodox Calvinism in a Netherlands church largely given over to a mild rationalism. Capadose practised medicine at the Hague, wrote against the smallpox vaccination of his day on grounds now generally thought mistaken, and spent his life in evangelistic and charitable work, in the cause of Jewish evangelisation, and in defence of the Reformed confessions against the liberal theology of the national church. He supported the seceders of 1834 in conscience while remaining within the establishment himself, and he laboured for the right of orthodox parents to Christian schools. “Brethren, my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved” (Rom 10:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a proselyte as a new convert to some religion, and awakening as a rousing from sleep, in a moral sense.
webster_full: PROS'ELYTE, n. A new convert to some religion or religious sect.
AWA'KENING, n. A revival of religion, or more general attention to religion.
PHYSI'CIAN, n. A person skilled in the art of healing; one whose profession is to prescribe remedies.
scriptures: Rom 10:1
Brethren, my heart's desire and prayer to God for Israel is, that they might be saved.
Rom 1:16
For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek.
Gal 2:20

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.
And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God.
corruption_summary: The Jewish physician whose 1822 baptism helped launch the Dutch Reveil.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Capadose's conversion is now sometimes treated as a cultural betrayal, the abandonment of a people for the religion of the majority. That reading misses both the cost and the content. He lost his standing and much of his family, and what he embraced was not Dutch respectability — the respectable church of the Netherlands was then rationalist — but the confessional Calvinism that respectable opinion despised.

The principle to recover is Paul's own position, which Capadose occupied: the gospel is “the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek” (Rom 1:16), and the apostle's heart's desire for Israel is a prayer, not a programme of pressure (Rom 10:1). His own account of his life was Paul's: “I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me” (Gal 2:20).

“to the Jew first, and also to the Greek” (Rom 1:16) — his own order of grace.
“yet not I, but Christ liveth in me” (Gal 2:20) — after 1822.

pos: n. (Hendrik Peter Scholte, 1805–1868, seceder minister, founder of Pella, Iowa)
etymology: Dutch Hendrik, from Old German Heimerich, ruler of the home; Scholte, a steward, a village headman.
biblical_def: Hendrik Peter Scholte was one of the four young Leiden students — with de Cock, van Velzen and Brummelkamp — whose consciences could not be reconciled to the Netherlands Reformed Church of the 1830s, in which the confessions were a formality and ministers subscribed them only as far as they agreed with Scripture. He led the Afscheiding, the Secession of 1834, in his own congregation at Doeveren, was repeatedly fined and had soldiers billeted in his house as punishment for holding services. In 1847, judging that the Netherlands offered neither liberty nor bread to his people, he led about eight hundred seceders to America and founded the town of Pella in Iowa, which he governed, owned a great deal of, and quarrelled with for the rest of his life; he was a lawyer, a land agent, a newspaper editor and a delegate to the Republican convention of 1860. The emigration was deliberately Abrahamic in self-understanding. “Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee” (Gen 12:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines emigration as the removal of inhabitants from one country to another, and a colony as a body of people drawn from the mother country to inhabit some distant place.
webster_full: EMIGRA'TION, n. Removal of inhabitants from one country or state to another, for the purpose of residence.
COL'ONY, n. A company or body of people transplanted from their mother country to a remote province.
SECES'SION, n. The act of withdrawing, particularly from fellowship and communion.
scriptures: Gen 12:1
Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:
Heb 11:8
By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went.
How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
corruption_summary: The Afscheiding minister who led eight hundred Dutch seceders to Pella, Iowa, in 1847.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Scholte is a complicated man and the record should say so: the courage that held services under fines and billeted soldiers is the same self-assurance that made him an awkward neighbour and a litigious town founder in Iowa. The Secession was carried by men of exactly that temper, because a milder one would have submitted in 1834.

The principle to recover is that such a going out is an act of faith and not of grievance: “By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out into a place which he should after receive for an inheritance, obeyed; and he went out, not knowing whither he went” (Heb 11:8). The scattered carry the word with them (Act 8:4), and they sing the Lord's song in a strange land even while asking how (Psa 137:4).

roots_lines: Hebrew yalak (H3212) — to go, walk, depart; Genesis 12:1.

“How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?” (Psa 137:4) — Pella's first winter.

pos: n. (Anthony Brummelkamp, 1811–1888, seceder minister and professor at Kampen)
etymology: Latin Antonius, a Roman family name; Dutch Brummelkamp, bramble-field.
biblical_def: Anthony Brummelkamp was one of the four Leiden students of the Afscheiding and the one who gave the seceded churches their trained ministry. Deposed from his charge at Hattem in 1835 for joining the Secession, fined and imprisoned for holding services, he began teaching students for the ministry in his own house at Arnhem — a private theological school that, with van Velzen's and de Cock's, became the Theological School at Kampen in 1854, where he taught until 1882. With his brother-in-law van Raalte he also organised and encouraged the Dutch emigration to Michigan and Iowa, publishing a widely read pamphlet on the subject in 1846, though he stayed himself. He was the most conciliatory of the four, worked to heal the breaches that repeatedly divided the seceders, and held for a church which was strict in doctrine and generous in temper. His labour at Arnhem and Kampen was the reason the Secession survived its founders: “the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a seminary as a place of education, and emigration as removal from one country to another for residence.
webster_full: SEM'INARY, n. A place of education; a school, academy or college.
EMIGRA'TION, n. Removal of inhabitants from one country to another, for the purpose of residence.
DEPO'SE, v.t. To divest of office; to deprive of an office or dignity.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.
Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.
corruption_summary: The Afscheiding's teacher, whose house school at Arnhem became the Kampen seminary.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Brummelkamp answers the usual objection to secession, that a people who leave an establishment lose the institutions that make a church durable — the training, the examination, the succession of ministers. He began with students in his own front room while under sentence, and twenty years later his movement had a seminary that is still teaching.

The principle to recover is that a church is not provided for until its ministry is: elders ordained in every church (Act 14:23) and every city (Tit 1:5), and the deposit committed “to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2). A secession that cannot do this is a protest with a congregation attached.
roots_summary: Greek paratithemi (G3908), to commit, entrust; kathistemi (G2525), to appoint; presbuterion (G4244), presbytery.
roots_lines: Greek kathistemi (G2525) — to appoint, set in order; Titus 1:5.
Greek cheirotoneo (G5500) — to ordain by vote; Acts 14:23.
Greek presbuterion (G4244) — the body of elders; 1 Timothy 4:14.

“ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5) — what the Secession had to provide for itself.
“the laying on of the hands of the presbytery” (1Ti 4:14) — a succession without an establishment.

pos: n. (Henry Danhof, 1879–1952, Grand Rapids minister, co-founder of the Protestant Reformed Churches)
etymology: Old German Heimerich, ruler of the home; Dutch Danhof, the fir-yard.
biblical_def: Henry Danhof was pastor of the First Christian Reformed Church of Kalamazoo and then of Grand Rapids, and with Herman Hoeksema and George Ophoff the founder of the Protestant Reformed Churches. The dispute was over common grace. Danhof and Hoeksema denied that God has any favour whatever toward the reprobate, that the restraint of sin in the unregenerate is an operation of grace, or that the gifts of civilisation are evidences of divine kindness to those who perish; the Christian Reformed Synod of Kalamazoo in 1924 affirmed the three points of common grace and in 1925 the two men were deposed. They left with their congregations and formed a new denomination in 1926, insisting that they were not innovating but holding Dort against a drift toward a general benevolence that would end in a general offer and a general atonement. Danhof himself left the Protestant Reformed body in 1929 after further disputes. The question is still live, and his side of it rests on texts like Romans: “Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be” (Rom 8:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grace as the free unmerited love and favour of God, and reprobate as one lost to virtue and religion, rejected of God.
webster_full: GRACE, n. The free unmerited love and favor of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
REP'ROBATE, n. A person abandoned to sin; one lost to virtue and religion; one rejected of God.
SCHISM, n. In church affairs, a division or separation among people of the same religious faith.
scriptures: Rom 8:7
Because the carnal mind is enmity against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be.
Joh 6:44
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
Eph 2:8
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Tit 2:11
For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men,
corruption_summary: The Grand Rapids minister deposed in 1925 for denying common grace, and a PRC founder.
corruption_paragraphs: The common-grace controversy is not settled by calling one side harsh and the other loose. Danhof's fear was concrete and has some warrant in the century since: that a doctrine of general divine favour toward all men tends, in practice, to soften the particularity of the atonement and then to make the church's cultural engagement its chief business. His opponents' fear was equally concrete: that a God with no kindness at all toward the reprobate cannot sincerely command them to repent.

The principle both sides professed, and which must govern the argument, is the sovereignty of grace in salvation: “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44); “For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8). Whatever common favour God shows in providence, it saves nobody.
roots_summary: Greek phronema (G5427), the mind, way of thinking; echthra (G2189), enmity; charis (G5485), grace.
roots_lines: Greek phronema (G5427) — mind, way of thinking; Romans 8:7.
Greek epiphaino (G2014) — to appear, shine forth; Titus 2:11.
usage: “the carnal mind is enmity against God” (Rom 8:7) — his case against common grace.
“No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (Joh 6:44) — the ground both sides claimed.
“it is the gift of God” (Eph 2:8) — whatever is granted in providence.

pos: n. (John Geddie, 1815–1872, Nova Scotian missionary to Aneityum in the New Hebrides)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Geddie, a Scots surname, probably from geddy, a pike.
biblical_def: John Geddie was born in Banff, raised in Pictou County, Nova Scotia, and ordained in the Presbyterian Church of Nova Scotia, which he persuaded over ten years of patient agitation to undertake a foreign mission of its own — the first such mission sent out by any Canadian church. He and his wife Charlotte landed on Aneityum in the New Hebrides in 1848, among people who had killed and eaten the previous visitors, and stayed twenty-four years. He learned the language, reduced it to writing, translated the whole New Testament into Aneityumese, trained native teachers who carried the gospel to the neighbouring islands, and lived to see the whole population of Aneityum profess Christianity and abandon cannibalism, infanticide and widow-strangling. The tablet behind the pulpit of the church there reads, in Aneityumese, that when he landed in 1848 there were no Christians, and when he left in 1872 there were no heathen. “I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth” (Isa 49:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a missionary as one sent to propagate religion, and heathen as a pagan, one who worships idols or is unacquainted with the true God.
webster_full: MIS'SIONARY, n. One sent to propagate religion; one sent to preach the gospel among the heathen.
HEA'THEN, n. A pagan; a gentile; one who worships idols, or is unacquainted with the true God.
TRANSLA'TION, n. The act of turning into another language; a version.

corruption_summary: The Nova Scotian who gave Aneityum its New Testament and saw an island turn.
corruption_paragraphs: Geddie is the kind of missionary whose record is now read as cultural destruction — a Westerner who ended a people's customs and replaced their religion. The customs he ended were cannibalism, the strangling of widows at their husbands' funerals, and the killing of unwanted infants, and he ended them by persuasion over twenty-four years, having first learned the language well enough to translate the New Testament into it.

The principle to recover is the promise that drew him: “I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth” (Isa 49:6). The commission reaches “unto the uttermost part of the earth” (Act 1:8), and the end of it is a multitude “of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Rev 7:9) — Aneityumese among them.

pos: n. (Thomas Witherow, 1824–1890, Irish Presbyterian professor and author of The Apostolic Church — Which Is It?)
etymology: Aramaic Te'oma, a twin; Witherow, from an Ulster place-name, the white row.
biblical_def: Thomas Witherow was minister at Maghera in county Londonderry and from 1865 professor of church history at Magee College, Londonderry, and later moderator of the General Assembly of the Presbyterian Church in Ireland. He wrote the standard histories of Irish Presbyterianism after Reid — the Historical and Literary Memorials of Presbyterianism in Ireland and Derry and Enniskillen in the Year 1689 — and completed and corrected much of the record Reid had left. His best-known work is a short book, The Apostolic Church — Which Is It?, first published in 1856 and reprinted continuously ever since: it sets out, in a hundred plain pages, the New Testament evidence for the independence of the local congregation under a plurality of elders, the parity of ministers, the right of the people in the choice of their officers, and courts of review — and argues that the church which answers to the apostolic description is the presbyterian one. Whatever the reader concludes, the method is right: the question is asked of Scripture. “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apostolic as pertaining to the apostles or taught by them, and parity as equality of rank or degree.
webster_full: APOSTOL'IC, a. Pertaining to the apostles; taught by the apostles; according to the doctrines of the apostles.
PAR'ITY, n. Equality; as parity of reason; equality of rank or degree.
MEMO'RIAL, n. That which preserves the memory of something; a monumental record.

corruption_summary: Magee's church historian, author of The Apostolic Church — Which Is It?
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Witherow's little book is still worth reading for its method rather than only its conclusion. He does not argue from the dignity of antiquity, the convenience of a system, or the sentiment of a tradition; he lists what the New Testament actually says about officers, ordination, and the people's part, and asks which existing church that description fits.

The principle to recover is the test itself: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). Scripture is profitable “for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness” (2Ti 3:16), which includes correcting a church's own government.
